newsitem.title: DUBAI: Ex-Dubai air cargo inactive but rates firmer.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Dubai air cargo inactive but rates firmer.

text.p: The Dubai air cargo market enters the usually peak year-end period with volumes still low and airlines and forwarders more uncertain than they have been for months about the direction the market is heading, a Reuter survey showed.

Rates to the United States have moved higher dragged up by stronger tariffs on the Europe-USA sector. Some airlines, which have seen their U.S. rates fall by as much as 40 percent in the past 18 months, are also making a concerted effort to enforce higher rates.

"The market out of Europe to the States has picked up dramatically. So for European airlines with Middle East offices selling North American destinations there has been upward pressure on rates," said the manager at a large European carrier dominant in the ex-Dubai cargo market.
"It is not so much the local market which is determining the rate increase, but rather the rates are being indirectly affected by Europe," he added.
Other carriers, including British Airways, are trying to stick to increased rates in the face of higher costs and slimmer margins.

Market players say the introduction of fuel surcharges and rate rises by some has made worse the uncertainty of the heavily over-serviced market which has seen a sharp drop in traditional sea-air business this year.

"The market is somewhat variable, there are a number of price increases and some fuel surcharges, which has made the market very unpredictable in the short term," said Chas Munn manager of British Airways World Cargo Middle East and South Asia.
The market was "going through one of those flat periods of the year" in terms of volumes,Munn said adding it was likely to stay this way until Christmas, when it traditionally eases.
"It's up one day and down the next. Its been fluctuating like crazy. This is supposed to be the peak season," EVA Air cargo manager Leonard Thyagarajan concurred.
"Three days in a week airlines have so much cargo they can't fit in any more, and the next they don't even have 100 kg," he added.
A host of international carriers, including Lufthansa, KLM Royal Dutch Airlines and Air France have announced fuel surcharges. Some are yet to come into effect.

Between November 1 and 20 Dubai-owned carrier Emirates is phasing in a 10 U.S. cents a kg surcharge on long-haul flights, and five cents a kg on some shorter-haul routes. In most parts of the Middle East, the surcharge takes effect on November 15.
Forwarders say they expect to have difficulty passing on the surcharges to shippers. Instead they are seeking alternative routings on airlines which have not yet introduced a surcharge.
"Customers are not going to be happy. We will try to use the airlines that haven't got a surcharge yet," an agent said.
Munn said BA had increased its rates to the USA on November 4 by between five and 15 percent.
Carriers hope the higher prices, whether in the form of rate increases or fuel surcharges, will help establish an upward trend in the longer term.
"All handling and distribution costs have gone up worldwide in the last 18 months and rates have been consistently dropping. This can't carry on without damaging business," Munn said.
Airlines had to invest in "vital" electronic data interchange but this would not be easy as long as rates continued to drop and costs rose Munn said adding that something has got to give.

Operators in the Dubai market say business, subdued for most of this year, is feeling the slow down in textile shipments from the Indian subcontinent and Far East as the quota period for U.S. and European imports nears its end.
Sea-air freight volumes have fallen sharply this year as cheaper direct services from the subcontinent and Far East encourage shippers there to bypass Dubai and use the quicker all-air movement.
Reuters calculates the average rate on a 100 kg shipment with a six-to-one volume-to-weight ratio to London Heathrow four fils firmer at 3.66 dirhams. The same average rate applies to Frankfurt.

The tariffs to the United States have improved markedly. The average rate to JKF in New York is 6.10 dirhams from 5.80 dirhams a kg six weeks ago and the rate to Los Angeles is also up at 7.15 dirhams from an average 6.60.
Rates on Far East routes remain stable, at an average 3.90 to both Singapore and Hong Kong.
The average rate on a 100 kg shipment to Nairobi is still within its normal five fil range at 3.95 dirhams a kg.

With Christmas and New Year coming up and then the Chinese New Year and Ramadan starting early in 1997, players say business is likely to remain slack for some time in the Dubai market. But they are still hopeful that the higher rates will be maintained. -- Dubai newsroom +9714-626990
